title: Caring for the carers
hook: an old text about nursing the sick that gives the patient homework too
tomorrow: does the very last thought before death really matter?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cave, a sick elder, and seven factors of awakening recited beside him. A chant at the bedside. Now, the people who stay by that bedside night after night.

At a funeral, people line up to hug the family. Somewhere in the kitchen, the one who did the night shifts for months is refilling the coffee. Who looks after her? The suttas have an odd answer. There's a pair of short texts about nursing the sick. One lists what makes a good nurse. Fine, expected. The other lists what makes a patient easy or hard to care for. The sick person gets homework. Why would a text about illness tell the one who's ill how to treat their nurse?
screen: `REFILLING THE COFFEE.` → `WHAT MAKES A GOOD NURSE.` → `THE PATIENT GETS HOMEWORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the list for the patient. Do what helps you heal. Know the right amount. Take your medicine. Tell your nurse honestly how you are, worse, better or the same. And bear pain with patience. And here's the list for the nurse: able to prepare medicine, knows what helps, cares with goodwill, not for gain, isn't put off by the mess of a sick body, and can lift the patient's spirits with talk of the teaching. Put the two lists side by side, and the puzzle solves itself. Care runs in both directions. Honest reports make the nurse's work possible: nobody can help with a pain that nobody mentions. The nurse isn't a machine that hands out comfort. She's a person who gets tired, who needs honest answers, and who needs her own work respected. The monastic rule book goes further. When a sick monk dies, his robes and bowl go to the ones who nursed him, because, it says, those who tend the sick have much to do. The carer is seen. So caring for the carers isn't an extra kindness on top of the real work. It's part of the same work. The person in the bed matters. So does the person in the chair beside it.
screen: `THE PATIENT'S LIST.` · `THE NURSE'S LIST.` · `CARE RUNS BOTH WAYS.` · `THE ROBES GO TO THE NURSE.` · then, large: `CARE FOR THE CARERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who looks after someone: a parent, a nurse, a friend with a sick partner. First, name one thing that would lighten their week. Next, name what might stop you offering it. Last, choose one small, real way around that, and hold that plan in mind as you breathe.
Caring for the carers: seeing the one in the chair beside the bed. The suttas give the patient duties, and the rule book gives the nurse the robes.
For today: care for the carers, who are part of the care, and so are you, if you're the one in the chair. Twenty-two of thirty, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist monasteries assign monks to nurse the sick, and lay Buddhists support hospice workers and family carers with food, chores and company; some temples hold sits or gatherings for carers and the bereaved.

myth: in the suttas, only the nurse has duties; the patient just receives
one text lists the patient's part too: take your medicine, tell the truth about how you are, bear pain patiently.
a good nurse, the text says, isn't put off by the mess of a sick body
that's on the nurse's list, along with caring for goodwill, not for gain.
looking after carers is a nice extra, separate from caring for the sick
the two lists show care runs both ways. the carer is part of the same work.

fork.setup: your friend has spent every evening for months helping his mom care for his little sister after surgery. his grades are slipping. what do the two lists suggest?
options: nothing; caring for family is his duty, and complaining would be selfish.
he's a carer who needs care too: someone should check on him and share the load.
he should stop helping at home so he can focus completely on school.
fork.reveal: the suttas give duties to both sides of the bed, and the rule book honors the nurse. the carer is seen, not used up.

original.note: Pali upatthaka: attendant, one who looks after; Ananda was the Buddha's.

trapdoor: what you thought: in caring for the dying, all the attention belongs to the patient.
what it means: the old texts give duties to the patient and the nurse, and honor the nurse's work. the carer counts too.
what a scholar hears: Anguttara Nikaya 5.123-124 (five qualities of an easy patient and of a good nurse); Vinaya, Mahavagga 8.27 (the dead monk's robes and bowl given to those who nursed him).

chat.says: funeral was today. ava's mom took care of her grandma for months and now she just sits there. now what?
options: bring food, take one chore off her list, and let her rest without having to host.
give her space. carers are used to being strong and would rather be left alone.
help her get back to her normal routine fast; that's the best way to heal.
chat.meaning: The old texts give both patient and nurse a part, and honor the one who did the nursing. The carer needs care too.

tie.story: The suttas list duties for patient and nurse alike, and the rule book gives a dead monk's robes to his nurses.

suttas.meaning: discourses of the Buddha, in the Pali texts

monastic rule book.meaning: the Vinaya, the code of discipline for monks and nuns

robes and bowl.meaning: a monk's few belongings: his robes and his alms bowl

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.123 and 5.124, Upatthaka Suttas (five qualities that make a patient easy to nurse; five qualities of a good nurse)
Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga 8.27 (when a sick monk dies, his robes and bowl are given to those who nursed him, since they have much to do)

notes: Puzzle shape: the odd detail is that the sutta gives the patient duties toward the nurse.

AN 5.123-124 paraphrased; confirm the five patient qualities (does what is beneficial, knows moderation, takes medicine, reports symptoms truthfully, endures pain) and the five nurse qualities (prepares medicine, knows what helps, nurses with goodwill not gain, not disgusted to clean up, can inspire the patient with Dhamma talk). The script treats the nurse as 'she' in one passage as a general example; the suttas speak of monks.
Vinaya Mv 8.27 (robes and bowl to the nurses): confirm the reference number and the reason given.
